title: NASA lit fires on purpose in empty space cargo ships to study flames

cover.alt: Bright yellow flames rise in two large clumps from a strip of burning material in a dark chamber, with a glowing wire stretched between them.
cover.credit: NASA Glenn Research Center · Public domain

body: A fire is one of the worst things that can happen on a spacecraft, but lighting big ones on a crewed station is far too risky. So between 2016 and January 2024, NASA’s six **Saffire** experiments burned samples inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo ships after they had left the International Space Station, before each ship burned up on re-entry. In weightlessness hot gas doesn’t rise, so there is no buoyant draught to feed a flame: [a candle in orbit](https://www.nasa.gov/image-detail/candle-flames-3/) becomes a blue sphere. Saffire’s flow unit therefore worked like a small wind tunnel, pushing air past the burning sample while cameras and sensors recorded how the fire grew.

slides.alt: In a dark chamber, yellow flames leap in two big clumps along a sheet of burning plastic, flickering upwards in the airflow, with thin glowing sensor wires across them. Suddenly they shrink to dim spots, turn faint blue and almost vanish.
slides.caption: Saffire-VI, NASA’s sixth fire experiment, inside an empty Cygnus cargo ship: flames spread over a sample of acrylic as air blows past. When the airflow is slowed, they shrink to a faint blue glow.
slides.credit: NASA Glenn Research Center · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: Why flames need help in orbit

left.label: On Earth
left.text: Hot gas rises and pulls fresh air in from below. That draught makes a candle flame a yellow teardrop.

right.label: In orbit
right.text: Nothing rises, so oxygen only creeps in slowly unless air is moved. Saffire blew air past its samples.

slides.label: the cotton and fibreglass sheet burned by Saffire-I in June 2016
slides.text: It was the first large fire lit on purpose inside an orbiting spacecraft. Earlier fire tests in space had used much smaller samples.

slides.heading: Eight years of fires in space
slides.note: Six experiments in all, each in a Cygnus after it left the space station

slides.heading: What the fires showed
slides.text: In the first three tests, flames spread fast but then held a steady size and burn rate; on Earth, similar fires tend to keep growing. The spacecraft’s size mattered more than expected. Saffire-VI, the last, ran 19 burns with more oxygen and lower pressure, to mimic crewed spacecraft.

slides.question: Why were the Saffire fires lit in Cygnus after it had left the space station?
options: To keep the station and crew safe
Fire is easier to film there
The station has no electricity spare
slides.explanation: Burning in a cargo ship that had already undocked kept the fires well away from the station, and the ship was due to burn up on re-entry anyway.

source.label: NASA: Flame burns out on NASA’s long-running spacecraft fire experiment
